answer.label: Not Ralph Waldo Emerson — anonymous 1930s newspaper wisdom
answer.authorDates: First printed 3 February 1934 · The Placer Herald, Auburn, California
answer.sourceLine: The line first appears as an unsigned newspaper filler in 1934 and only acquired Emerson’s name in 1955, in Jacob M. Braude’s Speaker’s Encyclopedia — more than seventy years after Emerson’s death, and it is found nowhere in his writings.

source.excerpt: Every minute you are angry, you lose sixty seconds of happiness.
trail: The earliest known printing is an unsigned filler in The Placer Herald, 3 February 1934 ↗, carrying no author’s name; it recurs as anonymous folk-wisdom through the 1930s.
Emerson’s name was first attached in 1955, in Jacob M. Braude’s Speaker’s Encyclopedia — 73 years after Emerson died, with no citation ↗.
Along the way it was also pinned on Mary Pickford (via Irving Hoffman, 1951) and on Hoffman himself (1953) ↗ — none substantiated.
The saying is absent from Emerson’s sourced quotations ↗.
source.cutTag: ↑ the earliest text carries no author at all
source.excerptNote: This is the wording of the earliest known appearance, an unsigned filler item. The popular Emerson version simply prefixes “For” and sometimes swaps in “you remain angry … sixty seconds of peace of mind.”
source.rightsNote: This is a short, anonymous aphorism in continuous print since 1934 with no identified author; there is no rights-holder to credit. Please don’t re-caption it as Emerson.

author.name: Jacob M. Braude
author.heading: The compiler who attached Emerson
author.bio: Jacob M. Braude (1896–1970) was a prolific American compiler of anthologies for public speakers, including the widely used Speaker’s Encyclopedia of Stories, Quotations, and Anecdotes (1955). According to Quote Investigator, that volume is the earliest known source to print this saying under Ralph Waldo Emerson’s name — offered without any citation. Speaker’s handbooks like his were a common vector for pinning anonymous sayings onto famous names.

misattribution.heading: Who it’s wrongly credited to
misattribution.intro: Emerson gets the credit almost everywhere online, but the timeline rules him out — and he wasn’t the only wrong name.

items.why: There is no source in Emerson’s works, and the line is absent from his sourced quotations ↗. The first credit to Emerson appears in Braude’s 1955 Speaker’s Encyclopedia ↗ — 73 years after his death in 1882.
Columnist Irving Hoffman credited Pickford in a 1951 Hollywood Reporter column ↗, but with no supporting evidence.
A 1953 Cincinnati Enquirer item credited Hoffman himself ↗, apparently a misreading of his earlier column.

misattribution.truthLine: The saying is anonymous folk-wisdom, in print since 1934 with no author; per Quote Investigator ↗, none of the famous names attached to it hold up.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Emerson
lead: The appeal of the line is its tidy arithmetic — a minute of anger literally costs you sixty seconds of happiness. That epigrammatic snap made it perfect newspaper filler in the 1930s, and later perfect for greeting cards, posters, and social feeds, which is exactly the material that accumulates famous names.

Emerson is a magnet for orphaned aphorisms about self-reliance, temperament, and living well. Once a quotation compiler printed his name beside it in 1955, later anthologies and the internet copied the credit forward — a textbook case of an attribution outrunning its evidence.
context.pull: A minute of anger for sixty seconds of happiness — too neat to have needed a famous author, but it got one anyway.
